title: Mode hopping via nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling in a synthetic antiferromagnet

paper_content.abstract:
Identifying nonlinear interactions among magnons is crucial for advancing the field of
magnonics and developing next-generation spintronic devices. In this work, we report the
experimental observation of nonlinear magnon mode hopping and hysteretic behavior in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). Under strong radio-frequency excitation, the magnon system exhibits abrupt
transitions between acoustic and optic modes, accompanied by GHz-scale frequency jumps—orders
of magnitude larger than previously reported in magnon-based hybrid systems. We further show
that this mode hopping is hysteretic, reflecting multistable nonlinear dynamics, and support these
findings through theory and micromagnetic simulations. These results establish a new regime of
nonlinear magnon dynamics, going beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight
the potential of SAFs as platforms for magnon-based frequency converters and switches for
information processing.
paper_content.introduction:
Nonlinear phenomena play a crucial role in a wide range of physical systems, offering deep insights
into complex interactions and emergent behaviors. From the turbulence of fluid dynamics1,2 to the formation
of solitons in optics2,3, nonlinear physics has advanced our understanding of many-body systems4 and
collective excitations5. In condensed matter physics, nonlinear interactions often give rise to unique
phenomena6–8 such as chaos, pattern formation9, and bifurcations10, all of which are essential for advancing
both fundamental theory11 and technological applications.

In magnonic systems, nonlinear physics has also been a focus of considerable attention due to its
potential for manipulating spin waves and enabling new functionalities in devices12,13. Nonlinear magnon
interactions14 have been predominantly explored through multi-magnon scattering, which can lead to
phenomena, such as magnon Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC)15–17, which is typically observed in
incoherent magnon interactions where the magnons have random phases. More recently, magnon
nonlinearity has been explored in hybrid systems18,19, where phase-defined coherent magnons couple with
other quasiparticles, such as phonons or photons20–25, giving rise to phenomena such as frequency bi-
stability26, gain-driven auto-oscillation27 and anticrossing gap closing28.

Direct nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions, however, remain far less understood. While several
recent reports have demonstrated nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling phenomena12,29–32, most of these
works have focused on spectral signatures such as frequency mixing or gap modulation33–37. What has not
yet been explored, and what we focus on here, is the emergence of mode hopping with hysteresis—an
abrupt transition between two magnon modes under strong drive.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate such nonlinear mode hopping in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). The SAF supports two distinct magnon modes: optic (high-frequency) and acoustic
(low-frequency) magnons. By tuning an external magnetic field, we coupled these modes and observed
anticrossing behavior, consistent with established strong coupling of two magnon modes. More importantly,
under strong RF excitation, we uncovered a series of nonlinear effects that constitute the central findings
of this work: (1) abrupt mode hopping between the optic and acoustic modes, accompanied by frequency
jumps up to 5 GHz; (2) pronounced hysteresis of the mode hopping depending on the field sweep direction;
and (3) a frequency redshift and closure of the anticrossing gap.

To understand these effects, we developed a theoretical model that qualitatively matches our
experimental results. The model shows that the observed nonlinearities stem from interactions among
propagating and Kittel magnon modes, both optic and acoustic branches. As the RF driving power increases,
these magnons then participate in a three-magnon process between the optic and acoustic modes, resulting
in the observed mode hopping and its hysteretic character. These findings advance the understanding of
nonlinear magnon dynamics beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight SAFs as a
promising platform for magnon-based switches and frequency converters where large GHz-scale jumps can
be exploited for information processing.
paper_content.results:
Samples and measurement set-up
For this study, we fabricated a sample with a SAF structure consisting of Ru (3 nm)/CoFeB (15
nm)/Ru (0.6 nm)/CoFeB (15 nm)/Pt (1 nm)/Ru (3 nm)/Ta (3 nm). The two CoFeB layers with in-plane
magnetization are separated by a 0.6 nm Ru spacer to induce antiferromagnetic coupling via the Ruderman-
Kittel-Kasuya-Yoshida (RKKY) interaction. The sample was patterned into a strip with dimensions of 10
μm in width and 100 μm in length, and a 60 nm-thick SiO insulating layer was deposited above the strip.
Finally, two coplanar waveguide (CPW) antennas were patterned on top of the insulating layer to generate
the RF driving field. The distance between the centers of the two CPW antennas was set to 1 μm, as shown
in Fig. 1(a) [see Methods and Supplementary Note S1 for details].

Figure 1(b) illustrates the schematic of our experimental setup. We drive an RF field through CPW1
to generate spin waves, which propagate towards CPW2 within external in-plane magnetic field at an angle
𝜃 respect to propagating direction. The transmitted spin waves are then detected using the S parameter
k 21
of a vector network analyzer (VNA). Since our sample has a SAF structure, it supports two distinct magnon
modes: the optic mode and the acoustic mode38, as depicted in Figs. 1(c) and 1(d). In the optic mode (Fig.
1c), the magnetizations of the two CoFeB layers precess out-of-phase, resulting in a higher frequency,
whereas in the acoustic mode (Fig. 1d), they precess in-phase, leading to a lower frequency. These two
modes can be selectively excited by adjusting the angle of the applied magnetic field. When the field is
applied at an angle of 0°, tilting the magnetization along the x-axis, RF excitation predominantly drives the
optic mode. Conversely, when the magnetic field is applied at 90°, tilting the magnetization along the y-
axis, the in-phase acoustic mode is excited [see Supplementary Fig. S1]. The crossing of two magnon modes
can be achieved when the magnetic field is applied at a 45° angle, where both modes are excited, resulting
in their coupling. This coupling is manifested as an anticrossing with large cooperativity [see
Supplementary Note 1] 33–35,37. The observation of anticrossing indicates that the propagating spin wave is
dominant in our measurement, rather than the non-propagating Kittel mode, since the coupling between
optic and acoustic modes in SAF occurs only for propagating spin waves through dynamic dipolar
interaction37. We note that, unlike previous reports on van der Waals magnets36—where an anticrossing gap
was observed by applying out-of-plane (OOP) magnetic field—our SAF system shows no such OOP-
induced anticrossing [see Supplementary Note 2], which can be attributed to the relatively weak interlayer
exchange field in our system36,39.

Nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling
We next investigate the nonlinear behavior of the magnon-magnon coupling. To do this, we fixed
the magnetic field angle at 45° and gradually increased the RF driving power while measuring the spin
wave spectra. To avoid the influence of magnetization switching, the sample was first saturated at positive
field and then returned to zero before increasing the field again [the effect of RF driving power on
magnetization switching is discussed in Supplementary Note 3]. As shown in Figs. 2(a)-(c), from -20 dBm
to 0 dBm, the spectra show minimal change, with the anticrossing behavior clearly visible. However, as the
driving power increases further, the spectra begin to distort, and nonlinear effects become apparent, as seen
in Figs. 2(d)-(f).

Several distinct nonlinear phenomena are observed for high RF driving power. First, above the
threshold, the overall resonant frequency experiences a redshift. Figure 2(g) quantifies this, showing the
magnon frequency as a function of driving power, where a sudden frequency drop occurs once the threshold
is exceeded. Second, we observe the closure of the anticrossing gap beyond this threshold. For clearer
visualization, Fig. 2(h) presents the frequency spectrum at the anticrossing point as the driving power
increases, showing the gradual closing of the gap. These observations—frequency redshift and gap
closure—suggest that the propagating magnons, which are primarily responsible for the frequency
anticrossing, weaken in the nonlinear regime, and the lower-frequency Kittel magnons may become
dominant.

Most notably, mode hopping is observed once the power exceeds the threshold. As we increase the
magnetic field, we observed that at around 20 mT—where the frequency of the optic magnon, 𝜔 , is

magnons may trigger an optic-to-acoustic mode transition via a three-magnon scattering process40,41, where
one optic magnon with 𝜔 splits into two acoustic magnons with 𝜔 . Importantly, additional

It should be noted that although our measurements employ a single excitation frequency, nonlinear
interactions between magnons at different frequencies can still manifest. Recent studies have clearly
demonstrated this point: ref. 29 showed that single-frequency FMR excitation in a SAF can nevertheless
reveal acoustic–optic three-magnon scattering, while ref. 42 reported nonlinear frequency doubling under
high-power drive using heterodyne MOKE. These findings establish that single-frequency measurements
can capture signatures of multi-frequency magnon interactions, consistent with the observed mode hopping.

Hysteretic behavior in nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling
To further investigate the nonlinear-induced mode hopping, we explore the field sweep direction
dependence, as hysteresis is commonly observed in nonlinear systems. Under the same experimental
conditions as before, we measured the spin wave spectra while sweeping the magnetic field forward
(increase) and backward (decrease). As shown in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b), below the threshold power (0 dBm),
there is no noticeable difference in the spin wave spectra for forward (Fig. 3a) or backward (Fig. 3b) field
sweeps. However, at an RF power of 2.5 dBm, which exceeds the threshold, the spin wave spectra exhibit
clear hysteresis, with the mode hopping point depending on the direction of the field sweep, as seen in Figs.
3(c) (forward) and 3(d) (backward).

To provide a more quantitative analysis, we extract the resonant frequencies from each spectrum
and plotted them as a function of magnetic field for forward (red) and backward (blue) sweep, as shown in
Figs. 3(e)-(h). As the power increases, we observe that the hysteresis gap gradually narrows: at 2.5 dBm,
the gap is approximately 15 mT (Fig. 3f), while at 10 dBm, the gap reduces to less than 5 mT (Fig. 3h). The
presence of hysteresis as well as the narrowing of the hysteresis gap suggests that the mode hopping process
involves more than a simple three-magnon scattering mechanism based on 𝜔 ≈ 2𝜔 and may involve
op ac
a more complex process.

paper_content.methods:
Film preparation and device fabrication
The Ru (3 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Ru (0.6 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Pt (1 nm)/ Ru (3 nm)/ Ta (3 nm)
synthetic antiferromagnetic film (illustrative sample stack is described at the Supplementary Note S1) were
deposited on Si/SiO (200 nm) substrates using AJA compact UHV sputtering system under a base pressure
2
of ~10-9 Torr. The working pressure was maintained at 3 mTorr with an Ar gas flow of 30 sccm into the
chamber. All the metallic layers were deposited by DC magnetron sputtering.

The film was patterned into the strip-line structure with dimensions of 10 µm in width and 100 µm
in length using photolithography (MicroWriter ML3 Baby, Durham Magneto Optics) and Ar ion milling
(KVET-B2000, KOREA VACUUM TECH) under a low base pressure of 7×10-7 Torr. The Ar ion beam
was generated by flowing 10 sccm Ar gas into the chamber, maintaining a working pressure of 0.5 mTorr.
On top of the pattern, we deposited the with 65 µm-width 90 µm-wide and 60 nm-thick SiO insulating
2
layer (blue region in Fig. 1a) to prevent flowing of leakage current from metallic sample to coplanar
waveguide (CPW) antennae.

The CPW antennae for the GSG contact were fabricated using a Ti (5 nm)/Au (150 nm) through
photolithography, following the same process as the sample patterning, while the central parts were
designed by E-beam lithography (TESCAN essence MIRA, EBL kit). After the lift-off process, the CPW
geometry is given by 1.28 µm-width signal-line and 0.68 µm-width ground-line. The centre-to-centre
distance between signal lines is 4.94 µm, while the shortest distance between ground lines is just 1 µm, as
illustrated in Fig. 1(a), with an enlarged view provided in Supplementary Fig. S1(d).

RF measurements set-up
The spin-wave spectra were measured using a vector network analyser (VNA), specifically the
Keysight PNA E5080, while applying an in-plane magnetic field. The RF-signal processing was conducted
over a frequency range of 100 MHz to 15 GHz, with IF-bandwidth of 500 Hz. The magnetic field was
applied using a customized in-plane electromagnet from KR-TECH (Korea), with a resolution of 0.1 mT.
The measurements were performed using a home-built probe station equipped with GSG probes and RF
measurement toolkits.

Data availability
The datasets generated and/or analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding
authors on reasonable request.

Code Availability
The relevant codes for numerical calculation/simulation of this work are available from corresponding
authors upon reasonable request.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Recently, magnon-magnon coupling in synthetic antiferromagnet has widely investigated experimentally, theoretically, and
micromagnetic simulations. In this work, the authors experimentally and theoretically the magnon-magnon coupling in SAF
and the high RF power induced nonlinear phenomenon. The observed mode hoping and the hysteretic behavior
phenomena is very interesting for the field of nonlinear magnonics. However, I cannot make a recommendation for the
current format of the manuscript. I suggest that the authors revise the manuscript with more focus on the mode hoping and
hysteretic behavior of magnon modes since the strong and even ultrastrong coupling between optical and acoustic magnons
in synthetic antiferromagnets have been already reported. Followings are my suggestions.
1.The hysteretic behavior of magnon mode should relate to the magnetization hysteresis loop. Is it possible to add a part on
discussing the effect of RF power on the static MH loops?
2.Micromagnetic simulations have been widely used to understand the coupling mechanism since it can provide the
direction precession information of different magnon modes. The observed “mode hoping” should be further understood with
the help of micromagnetic simulations.
3.Regarding the external magnetic field, here, the authors studied the directions of external magnetic field in the plane of
sample. Generally, the magnon-magnon coupling can also be realized by tilting the field toward out-of-plane direction. The
observed mode hoping can also appear when tilting the magnetic field out-of-plane? It is appreciated if they can give a
discussion.
4.The results and schematic presented in Fig. 1 are nothing new, I think these can be shown in supplemental, especially
Fig. 1e-f.
5.In Fig. 2, the angle of magnetic field should be indicated in the caption. In Fig. 2g, the label should be inserted.
6.Fig. 2h is used to present the observed closing of anticrossing gap. Is there a better field than 27 mT. I suggest they chose
the field at which the intensity of the optical and acoustic is similar.
7.In Fig. 3e-h, four typical RF power is provided. I am wondering that the RF power 2.5 dBm is the threshold for a specific
direction of external magnetic field or for all in-plane angles? The hysteretic behavior appears abruptly or slowly?
8.Since the results in Fig. 4 is theoretical calculations, is it possible give a discussion on how the threshold RF power
varying with extremal field? It is still not quite clear why the mode hopping decreases with G1? Is it related to the variation of
the precession angle of magnetizations (m, m1, m2)? Micromagnetic simulations should be helpful.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Mujin You and co-authors report strong coupling and nonlinear interactions involving two GHz-frequency
magnons in a synthetic antiferromagnetic structure driven by RF excitations. They observe a range of nonlinear effects
above a certain RF power threshold, including frequency shifts, anticrossing gap closure, mode hopping with large
frequency jumps, and hysteresis. The authors further develop a phenomenological model that considers nonlinear
interactions between Kittel and propagating magnon modes to explain their experimental findings. The manuscript is well-
written, and the study is scientifically sound. Therefore, I recommend that the paper be considered for publication in Nature
Communications, provided that the authors address the following questions:
1. Since the anticrossing originates from dipolar interactions, the size of the anticrossing gap is expected to depend on the
excitation wavevector and, consequently, the width of the coplanar waveguide. Could the authors clarify the influence of the
coplanar waveguide structure on the coupling and the nonlinear interactions observed?
2. What is the physical origin of the narrowing hysteresis gap with increasing RF power? While the numerical simulations
reproduce this effect as the magnonic gain G_1 increases, a detailed discussion of the underlying mechanism is also
needed.
3. The Hamiltonian in the theoretical model primarily considers three-magnon interactions to account for the observed
nonlinearities. Could four-magnon processes, such as magnon self-Kerr and cross-Kerr interactions, also play a role in the
observed phenomena? If so, could the authors comment on their potential contributions?
Minor point: The intensity scales should be defined in all the 2D color plots throughout Figures 1–3.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript reports a study of magnon spectra in a synthetic antiferromagnet under strong microwave excitation. The
authors show that with increasing excitation power, the spectrum undergoes strong modifications, which are described in
terms of nonlinear mode hoping and explained by magnon-magnon interaction. The observed modifications are hysteretic
and depend on the direction, in which the magnetic field is changed. The authors also present a model, that reproduces the
observed hysteresis.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend publication of this work for the following reasons:
1. First of all, the claims of novelty in the abstract and introduction are an exaggeration. In fact, there are many works
demonstrating nonlinear coupling between coherent magnons. One can mention Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) as
one of the recent examples. If the authors conduct a thorough literature search, they will find many more examples.
2. The interpretation of the results in terms of nonlinear coupling of coherent magnons is highly controversial.
a) All the considered “interacting” magnons (acoustic and optic Kittel magnons and propagating magnons) have different
frequencies. In the experiment, they are excited by sweeping the frequency of the microwave source, i.e., at different
moments in time. These magnons never coexist in the sample unless the frequency is swept on a temporal scale shorter
than the magnon relaxation time, which I believe is impossible. Therefore, the idea of the interaction of coherent magnons is
not applicable here. For such an interaction to exist, interacting magnons must be excited simultaneously by two sources (as
in Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) mentioned above).
b) Let us now consider the hysteresis (e.g., Fig. 3f). It appears that the state of the system found at 20 mT depends on
whether previous measurements were made at larger or smaller field. However, all magnons excited in these previous
measurements relax completely before the measurement at 20 mT is started. Therefore, the observed hysteretic behavior
cannot be due to the magnon accumulation. Obviously, it is caused by a process characterized by a much longer relaxation
time. For example, it can be caused by heating the sample with intense microwaves.

Response:
We thank the reviewer for recognizing the importance of our work and for suggesting that we more clearly
emphasize its distinction from earlier studies. Motivated by this valuable feedback, we have reformulated the
revised manuscript to focus on the mode hopping and hysteretic behavior of magnon modes, which represent
the central and novel aspects of our study. The main text and figures have been reorganized accordingly, and
additional discussion and data have been included to highlight these features. We hope that the reviewer finds

Comment 1. The hysteretic behavior of magnon mode should relate to the magnetization hysteresis loop. Is
it possible to add a part on discussing the effect of RF power on the static MH loops?
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As the reviewer pointed out, both the magnon mode
and the magnetization switching exhibit hysteretic behaviors, suggesting that they may be related. To clarify
this point, we performed magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurements of the magnetization hysteresis
loops. The schematic of the measurement setup is shown in Fig. R1a. The MOKE sensitivity was adjusted to
detect the magnetization along the x-axis, while the external magnetic field was applied at a 45° angle,
consistent with the magnon experiment. The results show that magnetization switching occurs at
approximately 5 mT. Considering that the magnon mode hopping appears above 10 mT, we conclude that
magnetization switching and magnon mode hopping are not directly correlated. In other words, when the
magnetic field is gradually increased, magnetization switching first occurs, and only after the magnetization
is well defined with respect to the field direction does the mode hopping emerge.
One may expect that the magnetization switching around 5 mT could affect the mode-hopping
measurements, as the field is swept from zero to positive values and thus abrupt changes might appear near 5
mT. However, we note that no signal change is observed around 5 mT in the f–H map (Fig. 3 in the main text).
This is because the sample was first saturated at positive field and then returned to zero before increasing the
field again (we have specified this in the revised manuscript). As a result, the magnon signal does not capture
any feature directly associated with the magnetization switching process.
To further address the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the effect of RF power on the static MH loops, we
measured MH loops while varying the RF excitation power. Although the ideal measurement would be
performed in between the two antennas where magnons are most strongly excited, the laser spot size was too
large to access this narrow region. Therefore, we performed the measurement just outside the right antenna.
According to a recent report by D. Hayashi et al. [Appl. Phys. Lett. 126, 082401 (2025)], nonlinear magnons
are also efficiently generated in the area just outside the antenna, ensuring that any influence of magnons on
the MH loops could still be detected.
RF signals ranging from –10 dBm to +10 dBm were applied to the coplanar waveguide (CPW) antenna
using a signal generator, and the MOKE signal was recorded at frequencies corresponding to nonlinear mode
hopping. As shown in Figs. R1b–d, the MH loops do not exhibit any noticeable change with increasing RF
power. This indicates that the influence of RF excitation on the static magnetization is minimal. We attribute
this to the different nature of the two measurements: RF excitation drives a time-dependent oscillation of the
magnetization, whereas the MH loop reflects the time-averaged static magnetization. As a result, even under
RF excitation, the static MH loop remains almost unchanged.
We have added a Supplementary Note 3 to provide detailed information on the negligible effect of RF
power on the magnetization hysteresis loop in the mode-hopping field regime.

Comment 3. Regarding the external magnetic field, here, the authors studied the directions of external
magnetic field in the plane of sample. Generally, the magnon-magnon coupling can also be realized by tilting
the field toward out-of-plane direction. The observed mode hoping can also appear when tilting the magnetic
field out-of-plane? It is appreciated if they can give a discussion.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. As the reviewer pointed out, out-of-plane (OOP)
magnetic fields can in some cases induce magnon–magnon coupling by lifting the degeneracy between optic
and acoustic modes [D. MacNeill et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 047204 (2019); A. H. Comstock et al., Nat.
Commun. 14, 1834 (2023)]. To clarify the role of OOP fields in our system, we conducted additional
measurements as follows.
First, we investigated whether magnon–magnon coupling could be induced in our SAF by applying a tilted
magnetic field. We measured FMR spectra with tilt angles of 90°, 60°, 30°, and 10° relative to the OOP
direction (see Fig. R1.3). Unlike previous reports on van der Waals magnets [e.g., Fig. 4 of MacNeill et al.,
PRL (2019); Fig. 3 of Comstock et al., Nat. Commun. (2023)], our measurements did not reveal any signature
of an anticrossing gap. Instead, we only observed a systematic shift of the mode crossing point toward higher
applied fields as the tilt angle increased, which we attribute to the change in the in-plane projection of the
external field. These results indicate that in our CoFeB/Ru/CoFeB SAF, an OOP field does not induce
symmetry breaking sufficient to generate magnon–magnon coupling.
Next, we examined whether an OOP field influences nonlinear mode hopping. We applied an OOP bias
field of 67 mT—comparable to the in-plane field used for mode-hopping measurements—and repeated the
experiments. As shown in Fig. R1.4, the spectra obtained with [Fig. R1.4b] and without [Fig. R1.4a] the OOP
field are nearly identical, confirming that the OOP field has negligible impact on mode hopping in our system.
We interpret these observations as follows. In our SAF, magnon–magnon coupling is mediated primarily
by dynamic dipolar interactions. The resulting anticrossing emerges when the magnetic field is applied in-
plane and is not collinear with the magnon propagation direction, providing the necessary symmetry breaking.
In contrast, prior studies of van der Waals antiferromagnets and low-symmetry layered magnets have shown
that OOP fields can break structural or parity symmetries, leading to gap opening. In those systems, intrinsic
asymmetries (e.g., inequivalent layers, inversion-symmetry breaking, or Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction)
allow OOP fields to couple the optic and acoustic modes.
Our CoFeB/Ru/CoFeB trilayer differs in key respects: the two ferromagnetic layers are nominally identical,
the Ru spacer only mediates interlayer exchange, and the system exhibits strong in-plane magnetic anisotropy.
As a result, the symmetry-breaking pathway for OOP-field–induced coupling is negligible. We therefore
conclude that in our SAF, the OOP magnetic field has negligible influence on both magnon–magnon coupling
and mode hopping.
We have added a Supplementary Note 2 to provide the discussion on the negligible effect of OOP field to
magnon-magnon coupling in our SAF.

Comment 6. Fig. 2h is used to present the observed closing of anticrossing gap. Is there a better field than 27
mT. I suggest they chose the field at which the intensity of the optic and acoustic is similar.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. As the reviewer pointed out, showing a line
profile where the optic and acoustic modes have comparable intensity would indeed provide a clearer
illustration of the gap closing. We also considered this point and examined line profiles at various fields (see
Fig. R1.5). Among the fields tested, 27 mT provided the clearest signature of both peaks, which is why we
presented this line profile in the main text.
While it would be ideal to find a field where the optic and acoustic intensities are nearly equal, such a
condition does not occur in our system. Both modes are present across the entire field range, but the intensity
of the upper branch is always larger. This asymmetry arises from the different origins of the two signals: in
our SAF, the optic mode intensity corresponds to variations of the longitudinal component of magnetization
along the external field direction, whereas the acoustic mode corresponds to variations of the transverse
component. At low fields (nearly spin-flop state), the spins align almost perpendicular to the field, so the
longitudinal variation is large while the transverse variation is small—resulting in strong optic and weak
acoustic signals. At high fields (nearly spin-flip state), the spins align nearly parallel to the field, so the
transverse variation becomes dominant while the longitudinal variation is suppressed—leading to strong
acoustic and weaker optic signals. Consequently, the upper branch remains stronger throughout the entire field
range. We note that this behavior is consistent with previous reports, for example Y. Shiota et al., Phys. Rev.
Lett. 125, 017203 (2020).

Reviewer #4
The manuscript reports a study of magnon spectra in a synthetic antiferromagnet under strong
microwave excitation. The authors show that with increasing excitation power, the spectrum undergoes
strong modifications, which are described in terms of nonlinear mode hoping and explained by magnon-
magnon interaction. The observed modifications are hysteretic and depend on the direction, in which
the magnetic field is changed. The authors also present a model, that reproduces the observed hysteresis.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend publication of this work for the following reasons:
Comment 1. First of all, the claims of novelty in the abstract and introduction are an exaggeration. In fact,
there are many works demonstrating nonlinear coupling between coherent magnons. One can mention Appl.
Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) as one of the recent examples. If the authors conduct a thorough literature
search, they will find many more examples.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment and agree that nonlinear coupling between coherent
magnons has been reported in a number of previous works, including Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022)
and others. Our intention was not to overstate novelty in this regard. Rather, the novelty of the present study
lies in the observation of nonlinear mode hopping and hysteretic behavior of magnon modes in SAFs, which,
to our knowledge, has not been previously reported.
Specifically, we demonstrate that under high RF power, the system exhibits an abrupt transition from the
optic to the acoustic mode, with a frequency drop as large as 4–5 GHz. We further show that this transition is
hysteretic, and we establish its microscopic origin through both theoretical modeling and micromagnetic
simulations. These features go beyond earlier demonstrations of nonlinear coupling by directly linking strong
nonlinearity to mode conversion and hysteresis.
Importantly, such abrupt and hysteretic mode conversion is not only of fundamental interest in nonlinear
magnonics but also carries potential for applications such as magnon-based mode converters and frequency
switches. Reviewer #1 also highlighted this point, noting that “the observed mode hopping and the hysteretic
behavior phenomena is very interesting for the field of nonlinear magnonics,” and the Editor likewise
recognized the significance of these findings.
We therefore believe that the focus of our work—on nonlinear mode hopping and hysteresis in SAFs—
provides a distinct and meaningful contribution that justifies consideration in Nature Communications. To
address this concern, we have revised the Abstract and Introduction to more clearly articulate that the novelty
of our work lies in the observation and explanation of nonlinear mode hopping and hysteresis, rather than in
magnon–magnon coupling itself.
Comment 2. The interpretation of the results in terms of nonlinear coupling of coherent magnons is highly
controversial.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that the interpretation of nonlinear magnon–magnon coupling remains
controversial. This is largely because the field is still at an early stage, and direct experimental evidence has
been limited. In the case of synthetic antiferromagnets (SAFs), the situation is further complicated by the
coexistence of optic and acoustic magnons, as well as the distinction between k = 0 Kittel magnons and
propagating magnons with k ≠ 0. Such complexity makes the manifestation of nonlinear effects diverse and
nontrivial.
Our study provides experimental evidence of nonlinear behaviors in SAFs, in particular magnon mode
hopping and hysteretic responses. Although the theoretical framework is not yet fully established, we believe
that presenting these experimental results is crucial for advancing understanding in this field. In particular,
they may help guide the development of a comprehensive theory and clarify the respective roles of Kittel and
propagating magnons in nonlinear coupling.
Below, we provide detailed responses to the reviewer’s specific comments. As the reviewer rightly
points out, some assumptions are unavoidable given the current state of the field, but we believe that our results will
contribute to the broader effort to build a comprehensive understanding of nonlinear magnon dynamics.
a) All the considered “interacting” magnons (acoustic and optic Kittel magnons and propagating magnons)
have different frequencies. In the experiment, they are excited by sweeping the frequency of the microwave
source, i.e., at different moments in time. These magnons never coexist in the sample unless the frequency is
swept on a temporal scale shorter than the magnon relaxation time, which I believe is impossible. Therefore,
the idea of the interaction of coherent magnons is not applicable here. For such an interaction to exist,
interacting magnons must be excited simultaneously by two sources (as in Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404
(2022) mentioned above).
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. It is correct that in our measurements we
excite and detect magnons at a single frequency. However, this does not necessarily mean that only single-
frequency magnons are involved; even in single-frequency measurements, the spectra can include signatures
of interactions among magnons at different frequencies. This has become increasingly clear from recent
studies, which demonstrate that nonlinear interactions can manifest under such measurement conditions.
For example, in a very recent work by A. Sud et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 246704 (2025)], which was
published during the revision of our manuscript, three-magnon scattering between acoustic and optic modes
in a SAF was directly observed using FMR. As shown in Figs. 2(c) and 2(d) of that paper, even though only
a single excitation frequency was applied, mode splitting occurred due to nonlinear three-magnon processes.
The authors demonstrated that strongly excited acoustic magnons can combine to generate optic magnons,
thereby giving rise to effective acoustic–optic coupling.
Similarly, D. Hayashi et al. [Appl. Phys. Lett. 126, 082401 (2025)], which was also published during the
revision of our manuscript, used heterodyne MOKE to study nonlinear effects in the same SAF system. Their
Fig. 3 clearly shows that excitation at frequency f produces a detectable signal at 2 f under high drive power,
rf rf
consistent with nonlinear up-conversion of acoustic magnons into optic magnons.
These reports indicate that, contrary to the reviewer’s concern, nonlinear interactions between magnons of
different frequencies can indeed appear in single-frequency measurements through three-magnon processes.
Our results should therefore be viewed in this broader context: while we excite at a single frequency, the
measured spectra can nevertheless reflect interactions involving magnons at multiple frequencies.
Taken together, these recent advances highlight that the understanding of nonlinear magnon interactions is
still developing, and we believe that our work contributes valuable experimental evidence toward building a
comprehensive picture of such processes in SAFs. In particular, our results extend beyond the conventional
focus on coherent k = 0 Kittel magnons by also capturing the crucial role of propagating magnons, thereby
providing a more comprehensive view of nonlinear magnon dynamics.
b) Let us now consider the hysteresis (e.g., Fig. 3f). It appears that the state of the system found at 20 mT
depends on whether previous measurements were made at larger or smaller field. However, all magnons
excited in these previous measurements relax completely before the measurement at 20 mT is started.
Therefore, the observed hysteretic behavior cannot be due to the magnon accumulation. Obviously, it is
caused by a process characterized by a much longer relaxation time. For example, it can be caused by heating
the sample with intense microwaves.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this critical comment. As the reviewer points out, the observation of
hysteresis in our SAF system implies a memory effect, which is a hallmark of nonlinear dynamics. In such
systems, multiple stable states can coexist, and the selected state depends on the sweep direction of the control
parameter.
In our case, strong nonlinear magnon–magnon coupling can give rise to multistable states associated with
either the optic or the acoustic mode. The presence of hysteresis therefore indicates that some form of memory
effect is at play. In our numerical calculations, different initial conditions were imposed depending on the
sweep direction, and hysteresis naturally emerged from this procedure. However, in our experiment, the origin
of the memory effect is not clear, because, as the reviewer mentioned, the magnons are completely relaxed
before the next measurement. Although the exact microscopic mechanism is not yet fully clear, one plausible
scenario is that the magnetization configuration at a given field differs slightly depending on the sweep
direction, and this difference biases the system toward a particular magnon mode.
To examine this possibility, we performed additional experiments by varying the in-plane field angle, since
different angles correspond to different magnetization configurations. The results (Fig. R4.1) show that the

This angle dependence suggests that the dominant magnon mode depends sensitively on the magnetization
state: at smaller 𝜃 angles the optic mode dominates (see Fig. 1c of the main text), whereas at larger angles

approaching 90° the acoustic mode is favored (Fig. 1d of the main text). This implies that even subtle
differences in the magnetization configuration, depending on the sweep direction, can determine which of the
two modes becomes stabilized and thus give rise to hysteresis in mode hopping.
We note that similar hysteretic memory effects have been reported in other nonlinear and hybrid magnonic
systems (e.g., Yao et al., PRL 130, 146702 (2023); Wang et al., PRL 120, 057202 (2018)), highlighting this
as an actively debated topic in the field. Our experimental evidence adds a valuable data point to this ongoing
discussion and may help elucidate the physics of nonlinear magnon–magnon coupling. Thus, while the exact
mechanism behind the memory effect in our SAF remains an open and potentially controversial question, our

Finally, we carefully evaluated the possibility of microwave-induced heating. If heating were significant,
one would expect observable changes in magnetization or anisotropy, detectable via MOKE. However, our

## Abstract

Identifying nonlinear interactions among magnons is crucial for advancing the field of
magnonics and developing next-generation spintronic devices. In this work, we report the
experimental observation of nonlinear magnon mode hopping and hysteretic behavior in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). Under strong radio-frequency excitation, the magnon system exhibits abrupt
transitions between acoustic and optic modes, accompanied by GHz-scale frequency jumps—orders
of magnitude larger than previously reported in magnon-based hybrid systems. We further show
that this mode hopping is hysteretic, reflecting multistable nonlinear dynamics, and support these
findings through theory and micromagnetic simulations. These results establish a new regime of
nonlinear magnon dynamics, going beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight
the potential of SAFs as platforms for magnon-based frequency converters and switches for
information processing.

---

## Introduction

Nonlinear phenomena play a crucial role in a wide range of physical systems, offering deep insights
into complex interactions and emergent behaviors. From the turbulence of fluid dynamics1,2 to the formation
of solitons in optics2,3, nonlinear physics has advanced our understanding of many-body systems4 and
collective excitations5. In condensed matter physics, nonlinear interactions often give rise to unique
phenomena6–8 such as chaos, pattern formation9, and bifurcations10, all of which are essential for advancing
both fundamental theory11 and technological applications.

In magnonic systems, nonlinear physics has also been a focus of considerable attention due to its
potential for manipulating spin waves and enabling new functionalities in devices12,13. Nonlinear magnon
interactions14 have been predominantly explored through multi-magnon scattering, which can lead to
phenomena, such as magnon Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC)15–17, which is typically observed in
incoherent magnon interactions where the magnons have random phases. More recently, magnon
nonlinearity has been explored in hybrid systems18,19, where phase-defined coherent magnons couple with
other quasiparticles, such as phonons or photons20–25, giving rise to phenomena such as frequency bi-
stability26, gain-driven auto-oscillation27 and anticrossing gap closing28.

Direct nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions, however, remain far less understood. While several
recent reports have demonstrated nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling phenomena12,29–32, most of these
works have focused on spectral signatures such as frequency mixing or gap modulation33–37. What has not
yet been explored, and what we focus on here, is the emergence of mode hopping with hysteresis—an
abrupt transition between two magnon modes under strong drive.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate such nonlinear mode hopping in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). The SAF supports two distinct magnon modes: optic (high-frequency) and acoustic
(low-frequency) magnons. By tuning an external magnetic field, we coupled these modes and observed
anticrossing behavior, consistent with established strong coupling of two magnon modes. More importantly,
under strong RF excitation, we uncovered a series of nonlinear effects that constitute the central findings
of this work: (1) abrupt mode hopping between the optic and acoustic modes, accompanied by frequency
jumps up to 5 GHz; (2) pronounced hysteresis of the mode hopping depending on the field sweep direction;
and (3) a frequency redshift and closure of the anticrossing gap.

To understand these effects, we developed a theoretical model that qualitatively matches our
experimental results. The model shows that the observed nonlinearities stem from interactions among
propagating and Kittel magnon modes, both optic and acoustic branches. As the RF driving power increases,
these magnons then participate in a three-magnon process between the optic and acoustic modes, resulting
in the observed mode hopping and its hysteretic character. These findings advance the understanding of
nonlinear magnon dynamics beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight SAFs as a
promising platform for magnon-based switches and frequency converters where large GHz-scale jumps can
be exploited for information processing.

## Results

Samples and measurement set-up
For this study, we fabricated a sample with a SAF structure consisting of Ru (3 nm)/CoFeB (15
nm)/Ru (0.6 nm)/CoFeB (15 nm)/Pt (1 nm)/Ru (3 nm)/Ta (3 nm). The two CoFeB layers with in-plane
magnetization are separated by a 0.6 nm Ru spacer to induce antiferromagnetic coupling via the Ruderman-
Kittel-Kasuya-Yoshida (RKKY) interaction. The sample was patterned into a strip with dimensions of 10
μm in width and 100 μm in length, and a 60 nm-thick SiO insulating layer was deposited above the strip.
Finally, two coplanar waveguide (CPW) antennas were patterned on top of the insulating layer to generate
the RF driving field. The distance between the centers of the two CPW antennas was set to 1 μm, as shown
in Fig. 1(a) [see Methods and Supplementary Note S1 for details].

Figure 1(b) illustrates the schematic of our experimental setup. We drive an RF field through CPW1
to generate spin waves, which propagate towards CPW2 within external in-plane magnetic field at an angle
𝜃 respect to propagating direction. The transmitted spin waves are then detected using the S parameter
k 21
of a vector network analyzer (VNA). Since our sample has a SAF structure, it supports two distinct magnon
modes: the optic mode and the acoustic mode38, as depicted in Figs. 1(c) and 1(d). In the optic mode (Fig.
1c), the magnetizations of the two CoFeB layers precess out-of-phase, resulting in a higher frequency,
whereas in the acoustic mode (Fig. 1d), they precess in-phase, leading to a lower frequency. These two
modes can be selectively excited by adjusting the angle of the applied magnetic field. When the field is
applied at an angle of 0°, tilting the magnetization along the x-axis, RF excitation predominantly drives the
optic mode. Conversely, when the magnetic field is applied at 90°, tilting the magnetization along the y-
axis, the in-phase acoustic mode is excited [see Supplementary Fig. S1]. The crossing of two magnon modes
can be achieved when the magnetic field is applied at a 45° angle, where both modes are excited, resulting
in their coupling. This coupling is manifested as an anticrossing with large cooperativity [see
Supplementary Note 1] 33–35,37. The observation of anticrossing indicates that the propagating spin wave is
dominant in our measurement, rather than the non-propagating Kittel mode, since the coupling between
optic and acoustic modes in SAF occurs only for propagating spin waves through dynamic dipolar
interaction37. We note that, unlike previous reports on van der Waals magnets36—where an anticrossing gap
was observed by applying out-of-plane (OOP) magnetic field—our SAF system shows no such OOP-
induced anticrossing [see Supplementary Note 2], which can be attributed to the relatively weak interlayer
exchange field in our system36,39.

Nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling
We next investigate the nonlinear behavior of the magnon-magnon coupling. To do this, we fixed
the magnetic field angle at 45° and gradually increased the RF driving power while measuring the spin
wave spectra. To avoid the influence of magnetization switching, the sample was first saturated at positive
field and then returned to zero before increasing the field again [the effect of RF driving power on
magnetization switching is discussed in Supplementary Note 3]. As shown in Figs. 2(a)-(c), from -20 dBm
to 0 dBm, the spectra show minimal change, with the anticrossing behavior clearly visible. However, as the
driving power increases further, the spectra begin to distort, and nonlinear effects become apparent, as seen
in Figs. 2(d)-(f).

Several distinct nonlinear phenomena are observed for high RF driving power. First, above the
threshold, the overall resonant frequency experiences a redshift. Figure 2(g) quantifies this, showing the
magnon frequency as a function of driving power, where a sudden frequency drop occurs once the threshold
is exceeded. Second, we observe the closure of the anticrossing gap beyond this threshold. For clearer
visualization, Fig. 2(h) presents the frequency spectrum at the anticrossing point as the driving power
increases, showing the gradual closing of the gap. These observations—frequency redshift and gap
closure—suggest that the propagating magnons, which are primarily responsible for the frequency
anticrossing, weaken in the nonlinear regime, and the lower-frequency Kittel magnons may become
dominant.

Most notably, mode hopping is observed once the power exceeds the threshold. As we increase the
magnetic field, we observed that at around 20 mT—where the frequency of the optic magnon, 𝜔 , is

nearly twice that of the acoustic magnon, 𝜔 , —the optic mode abruptly transitions into the acoustic mode

It should be noted that although our measurements employ a single excitation frequency, nonlinear

demonstrated this point: ref. 29 showed that single-frequency FMR excitation in a SAF can nevertheless
reveal acoustic–optic three-magnon scattering, while ref. 42 reported nonlinear frequency doubling under
high-power drive using heterodyne MOKE. These findings establish that single-frequency measurements
can capture signatures of multi-frequency magnon interactions, consistent with the observed mode hopping.

To further investigate the nonlinear-induced mode hopping, we explore the field sweep direction

Film preparation and device fabrication
The Ru (3 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Ru (0.6 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Pt (1 nm)/ Ru (3 nm)/ Ta (3 nm)
synthetic antiferromagnetic film (illustrative sample stack is described at the Supplementary Note S1) were
deposited on Si/SiO (200 nm) substrates using AJA compact UHV sputtering system under a base pressure
2
of ~10-9 Torr. The working pressure was maintained at 3 mTorr with an Ar gas flow of 30 sccm into the
chamber. All the metallic layers were deposited by DC magnetron sputtering.

The film was patterned into the strip-line structure with dimensions of 10 µm in width and 100 µm
in length using photolithography (MicroWriter ML3 Baby, Durham Magneto Optics) and Ar ion milling
(KVET-B2000, KOREA VACUUM TECH) under a low base pressure of 7×10-7 Torr. The Ar ion beam
was generated by flowing 10 sccm Ar gas into the chamber, maintaining a working pressure of 0.5 mTorr.
On top of the pattern, we deposited the with 65 µm-width 90 µm-wide and 60 nm-thick SiO insulating
2
layer (blue region in Fig. 1a) to prevent flowing of leakage current from metallic sample to coplanar
waveguide (CPW) antennae.

The CPW antennae for the GSG contact were fabricated using a Ti (5 nm)/Au (150 nm) through
photolithography, following the same process as the sample patterning, while the central parts were
designed by E-beam lithography (TESCAN essence MIRA, EBL kit). After the lift-off process, the CPW
geometry is given by 1.28 µm-width signal-line and 0.68 µm-width ground-line. The centre-to-centre
distance between signal lines is 4.94 µm, while the shortest distance between ground lines is just 1 µm, as
illustrated in Fig. 1(a), with an enlarged view provided in Supplementary Fig. S1(d).

The spin-wave spectra were measured using a vector network analyser (VNA), specifically the
Keysight PNA E5080, while applying an in-plane magnetic field. The RF-signal processing was conducted
over a frequency range of 100 MHz to 15 GHz, with IF-bandwidth of 500 Hz. The magnetic field was
applied using a customized in-plane electromagnet from KR-TECH (Korea), with a resolution of 0.1 mT.
The measurements were performed using a home-built probe station equipped with GSG probes and RF
measurement toolkits.

Data availability
The datasets generated and/or analyzed during the current study are available from the corresponding
authors on reasonable request.

authors upon reasonable request.

magnons in a synthetic antiferromagnetic structure driven by RF excitations. They observe a range of nonlinear effects
above a certain RF power threshold, including frequency shifts, anticrossing gap closure, mode hopping with large
frequency jumps, and hysteresis. The authors further develop a phenomenological model that considers nonlinear
interactions between Kittel and propagating magnon modes to explain their experimental findings. The manuscript is well-
written, and the study is scientifically sound. Therefore, I recommend that the paper be considered for publication in Nature
Communications, provided that the authors address the following questions:
1. Since the anticrossing originates from dipolar interactions, the size of the anticrossing gap is expected to depend on the
excitation wavevector and, consequently, the width of the coplanar waveguide. Could the authors clarify the influence of the
coplanar waveguide structure on the coupling and the nonlinear interactions observed?
2. What is the physical origin of the narrowing hysteresis gap with increasing RF power? While the numerical simulations
reproduce this effect as the magnonic gain G_1 increases, a detailed discussion of the underlying mechanism is also
needed.
3. The Hamiltonian in the theoretical model primarily considers three-magnon interactions to account for the observed
nonlinearities. Could four-magnon processes, such as magnon self-Kerr and cross-Kerr interactions, also play a role in the
observed phenomena? If so, could the authors comment on their potential contributions?
Minor point: The intensity scales should be defined in all the 2D color plots throughout Figures 1–3.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript reports a study of magnon spectra in a synthetic antiferromagnet under strong microwave excitation. The
authors show that with increasing excitation power, the spectrum undergoes strong modifications, which are described in
terms of nonlinear mode hoping and explained by magnon-magnon interaction. The observed modifications are hysteretic
and depend on the direction, in which the magnetic field is changed. The authors also present a model, that reproduces the
observed hysteresis.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend publication of this work for the following reasons:
1. First of all, the claims of novelty in the abstract and introduction are an exaggeration. In fact, there are many works
demonstrating nonlinear coupling between coherent magnons. One can mention Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) as
one of the recent examples. If the authors conduct a thorough literature search, they will find many more examples.
2. The interpretation of the results in terms of nonlinear coupling of coherent magnons is highly controversial.
a) All the considered “interacting” magnons (acoustic and optic Kittel magnons and propagating magnons) have different
frequencies. In the experiment, they are excited by sweeping the frequency of the microwave source, i.e., at different
moments in time. These magnons never coexist in the sample unless the frequency is swept on a temporal scale shorter
than the magnon relaxation time, which I believe is impossible. Therefore, the idea of the interaction of coherent magnons is
not applicable here. For such an interaction to exist, interacting magnons must be excited simultaneously by two sources (as
in Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) mentioned above).
b) Let us now consider the hysteresis (e.g., Fig. 3f). It appears that the state of the system found at 20 mT depends on
whether previous measurements were made at larger or smaller field. However, all magnons excited in these previous
measurements relax completely before the measurement at 20 mT is started. Therefore, the observed hysteretic behavior
cannot be due to the magnon accumulation. Obviously, it is caused by a process characterized by a much longer relaxation
time. For example, it can be caused by heating the sample with intense microwaves.

## Paper

## Abstract

Identifying nonlinear interactions among magnons is crucial for advancing the field of
magnonics and developing next-generation spintronic devices. In this work, we report the
experimental observation of nonlinear magnon mode hopping and hysteretic behavior in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). Under strong radio-frequency excitation, the magnon system exhibits abrupt
transitions between acoustic and optic modes, accompanied by GHz-scale frequency jumps—orders
of magnitude larger than previously reported in magnon-based hybrid systems. We further show
that this mode hopping is hysteretic, reflecting multistable nonlinear dynamics, and support these
findings through theory and micromagnetic simulations. These results establish a new regime of
nonlinear magnon dynamics, going beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight
the potential of SAFs as platforms for magnon-based frequency converters and switches for
information processing.

## Introduction

Nonlinear phenomena play a crucial role in a wide range of physical systems, offering deep insights
into complex interactions and emergent behaviors. From the turbulence of fluid dynamics1,2 to the formation
of solitons in optics2,3, nonlinear physics has advanced our understanding of many-body systems4 and
collective excitations5. In condensed matter physics, nonlinear interactions often give rise to unique
phenomena6–8 such as chaos, pattern formation9, and bifurcations10, all of which are essential for advancing
both fundamental theory11 and technological applications.

In magnonic systems, nonlinear physics has also been a focus of considerable attention due to its
potential for manipulating spin waves and enabling new functionalities in devices12,13. Nonlinear magnon
interactions14 have been predominantly explored through multi-magnon scattering, which can lead to
phenomena, such as magnon Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC)15–17, which is typically observed in
incoherent magnon interactions where the magnons have random phases. More recently, magnon
nonlinearity has been explored in hybrid systems18,19, where phase-defined coherent magnons couple with
other quasiparticles, such as phonons or photons20–25, giving rise to phenomena such as frequency bi-
stability26, gain-driven auto-oscillation27 and anticrossing gap closing28.

Direct nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions, however, remain far less understood. While several
recent reports have demonstrated nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling phenomena12,29–32, most of these
works have focused on spectral signatures such as frequency mixing or gap modulation33–37. What has not
yet been explored, and what we focus on here, is the emergence of mode hopping with hysteresis—an
abrupt transition between two magnon modes under strong drive.

In this work, we experimentally demonstrate such nonlinear mode hopping in a synthetic
antiferromagnet (SAF). The SAF supports two distinct magnon modes: optic (high-frequency) and acoustic
(low-frequency) magnons. By tuning an external magnetic field, we coupled these modes and observed
anticrossing behavior, consistent with established strong coupling of two magnon modes. More importantly,
under strong RF excitation, we uncovered a series of nonlinear effects that constitute the central findings
of this work: (1) abrupt mode hopping between the optic and acoustic modes, accompanied by frequency
jumps up to 5 GHz; (2) pronounced hysteresis of the mode hopping depending on the field sweep direction;
and (3) a frequency redshift and closure of the anticrossing gap.

To understand these effects, we developed a theoretical model that qualitatively matches our
experimental results. The model shows that the observed nonlinearities stem from interactions among
propagating and Kittel magnon modes, both optic and acoustic branches. As the RF driving power increases,
these magnons then participate in a three-magnon process between the optic and acoustic modes, resulting
in the observed mode hopping and its hysteretic character. These findings advance the understanding of
nonlinear magnon dynamics beyond previously reported strong-coupling effects, and highlight SAFs as a
promising platform for magnon-based switches and frequency converters where large GHz-scale jumps can
be exploited for information processing.

## Results

Samples and measurement set-up
For this study, we fabricated a sample with a SAF structure consisting of Ru (3 nm)/CoFeB (15
nm)/Ru (0.6 nm)/CoFeB (15 nm)/Pt (1 nm)/Ru (3 nm)/Ta (3 nm). The two CoFeB layers with in-plane
magnetization are separated by a 0.6 nm Ru spacer to induce antiferromagnetic coupling via the Ruderman-
Kittel-Kasuya-Yoshida (RKKY) interaction. The sample was patterned into a strip with dimensions of 10
μm in width and 100 μm in length, and a 60 nm-thick SiO insulating layer was deposited above the strip.
Finally, two coplanar waveguide (CPW) antennas were patterned on top of the insulating layer to generate
the RF driving field. The distance between the centers of the two CPW antennas was set to 1 μm, as shown
in Fig. 1(a) [see Methods and Supplementary Note S1 for details].

𝜃 respect to propagating direction. The transmitted spin waves are then detected using the S parameter
k 21
of a vector network analyzer (VNA). Since our sample has a SAF structure, it supports two distinct magnon
modes: the optic mode and the acoustic mode38, as depicted in Figs. 1(c) and 1(d). In the optic mode (Fig.
1c), the magnetizations of the two CoFeB layers precess out-of-phase, resulting in a higher frequency,
whereas in the acoustic mode (Fig. 1d), they precess in-phase, leading to a lower frequency. These two
modes can be selectively excited by adjusting the angle of the applied magnetic field. When the field is
applied at an angle of 0°, tilting the magnetization along the x-axis, RF excitation predominantly drives the
optic mode. Conversely, when the magnetic field is applied at 90°, tilting the magnetization along the y-
axis, the in-phase acoustic mode is excited [see Supplementary Fig. S1]. The crossing of two magnon modes
can be achieved when the magnetic field is applied at a 45° angle, where both modes are excited, resulting
in their coupling. This coupling is manifested as an anticrossing with large cooperativity [see
Supplementary Note 1] 33–35,37. The observation of anticrossing indicates that the propagating spin wave is
dominant in our measurement, rather than the non-propagating Kittel mode, since the coupling between
optic and acoustic modes in SAF occurs only for propagating spin waves through dynamic dipolar
interaction37. We note that, unlike previous reports on van der Waals magnets36—where an anticrossing gap
was observed by applying out-of-plane (OOP) magnetic field—our SAF system shows no such OOP-
induced anticrossing [see Supplementary Note 2], which can be attributed to the relatively weak interlayer
exchange field in our system36,39.

Nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling

the magnetic field angle at 45° and gradually increased the RF driving power while measuring the spin

Film preparation and device fabrication
The Ru (3 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Ru (0.6 nm)/ CoFeB (15 nm)/ Pt (1 nm)/ Ru (3 nm)/ Ta (3 nm)
synthetic antiferromagnetic film (illustrative sample stack is described at the Supplementary Note S1) were

2
of ~10-9 Torr. The working pressure was maintained at 3 mTorr with an Ar gas flow of 30 sccm into the
chamber. All the metallic layers were deposited by DC magnetron sputtering.

The film was patterned into the strip-line structure with dimensions of 10 µm in width and 100 µm
in length using photolithography (MicroWriter ML3 Baby, Durham Magneto Optics) and Ar ion milling
(KVET-B2000, KOREA VACUUM TECH) under a low base pressure of 7×10-7 Torr. The Ar ion beam
was generated by flowing 10 sccm Ar gas into the chamber, maintaining a working pressure of 0.5 mTorr.
On top of the pattern, we deposited the with 65 µm-width 90 µm-wide and 60 nm-thick SiO insulating
2
layer (blue region in Fig. 1a) to prevent flowing of leakage current from metallic sample to coplanar
waveguide (CPW) antennae.

The CPW antennae for the GSG contact were fabricated using a Ti (5 nm)/Au (150 nm) through

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, Mujin You and co-authors report strong coupling and nonlinear interactions involving two GHz-frequency
magnons in a synthetic antiferromagnetic structure driven by RF excitations. They observe a range of nonlinear effects
above a certain RF power threshold, including frequency shifts, anticrossing gap closure, mode hopping with large
frequency jumps, and hysteresis. The authors further develop a phenomenological model that considers nonlinear
interactions between Kittel and propagating magnon modes to explain their experimental findings. The manuscript is well-
written, and the study is scientifically sound. Therefore, I recommend that the paper be considered for publication in Nature
Communications, provided that the authors address the following questions:
1. Since the anticrossing originates from dipolar interactions, the size of the anticrossing gap is expected to depend on the
excitation wavevector and, consequently, the width of the coplanar waveguide. Could the authors clarify the influence of the
coplanar waveguide structure on the coupling and the nonlinear interactions observed?
2. What is the physical origin of the narrowing hysteresis gap with increasing RF power? While the numerical simulations
reproduce this effect as the magnonic gain G_1 increases, a detailed discussion of the underlying mechanism is also
needed.
3. The Hamiltonian in the theoretical model primarily considers three-magnon interactions to account for the observed
nonlinearities. Could four-magnon processes, such as magnon self-Kerr and cross-Kerr interactions, also play a role in the
observed phenomena? If so, could the authors comment on their potential contributions?
Minor point: The intensity scales should be defined in all the 2D color plots throughout Figures 1–3.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript reports a study of magnon spectra in a synthetic antiferromagnet under strong microwave excitation. The
authors show that with increasing excitation power, the spectrum undergoes strong modifications, which are described in
terms of nonlinear mode hoping and explained by magnon-magnon interaction. The observed modifications are hysteretic
and depend on the direction, in which the magnetic field is changed. The authors also present a model, that reproduces the
observed hysteresis.
Unfortunately, I cannot recommend publication of this work for the following reasons:
1. First of all, the claims of novelty in the abstract and introduction are an exaggeration. In fact, there are many works
demonstrating nonlinear coupling between coherent magnons. One can mention Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) as
one of the recent examples. If the authors conduct a thorough literature search, they will find many more examples.
2. The interpretation of the results in terms of nonlinear coupling of coherent magnons is highly controversial.
a) All the considered “interacting” magnons (acoustic and optic Kittel magnons and propagating magnons) have different
frequencies. In the experiment, they are excited by sweeping the frequency of the microwave source, i.e., at different
moments in time. These magnons never coexist in the sample unless the frequency is swept on a temporal scale shorter
than the magnon relaxation time, which I believe is impossible. Therefore, the idea of the interaction of coherent magnons is
not applicable here. For such an interaction to exist, interacting magnons must be excited simultaneously by two sources (as
in Appl. Phys. Lett. 121, 112404 (2022) mentioned above).
b) Let us now consider the hysteresis (e.g., Fig. 3f). It appears that the state of the system found at 20 mT depends on
whether previous measurements were made at larger or smaller field. However, all magnons excited in these previous
measurements relax completely before the measurement at 20 mT is started. Therefore, the observed hysteretic behavior
cannot be due to the magnon accumulation. Obviously, it is caused by a process characterized by a much longer relaxation
time. For example, it can be caused by heating the sample with intense microwaves.

Comment 1. The hysteretic behavior of magnon mode should relate to the magnetization hysteresis loop. Is

Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As the reviewer pointed out, both the magnon mode
and the magnetization switching exhibit hysteretic behaviors, suggesting that they may be related. To clarify
this point, we performed magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) measurements of the magnetization hysteresis
loops. The schematic of the measurement setup is shown in Fig. R1a. The MOKE sensitivity was adjusted to
detect the magnetization along the x-axis, while the external magnetic field was applied at a 45° angle,
consistent with the magnon experiment. The results show that magnetization switching occurs at
approximately 5 mT. Considering that the magnon mode hopping appears above 10 mT, we conclude that
magnetization switching and magnon mode hopping are not directly correlated. In other words, when the
magnetic field is gradually increased, magnetization switching first occurs, and only after the magnetization
is well defined with respect to the field direction does the mode hopping emerge.
One may expect that the magnetization switching around 5 mT could affect the mode-hopping
measurements, as the field is swept from zero to positive values and thus abrupt changes might appear near 5
mT. However, we note that no signal change is observed around 5 mT in the f–H map (Fig. 3 in the main text).
This is because the sample was first saturated at positive field and then returned to zero before increasing the
field again (we have specified this in the revised manuscript). As a result, the magnon signal does not capture
any feature directly associated with the magnetization switching process.
To further address the reviewer’s suggestion regarding the effect of RF power on the static MH loops, we
measured MH loops while varying the RF excitation power. Although the ideal measurement would be
performed in between the two antennas where magnons are most strongly excited, the laser spot size was too
large to access this narrow region. Therefore, we performed the measurement just outside the right antenna.
According to a recent report by D. Hayashi et al. [Appl. Phys. Lett. 126, 082401 (2025)], nonlinear magnons
are also efficiently generated in the area just outside the antenna, ensuring that any influence of magnons on
the MH loops could still be detected.
RF signals ranging from –10 dBm to +10 dBm were applied to the coplanar waveguide (CPW) antenna
using a signal generator, and the MOKE signal was recorded at frequencies corresponding to nonlinear mode
hopping. As shown in Figs. R1b–d, the MH loops do not exhibit any noticeable change with increasing RF
power. This indicates that the influence of RF excitation on the static magnetization is minimal. We attribute
this to the different nature of the two measurements: RF excitation drives a time-dependent oscillation of the
magnetization, whereas the MH loop reflects the time-averaged static magnetization. As a result, even under
RF excitation, the static MH loop remains almost unchanged.

Comment 3. Regarding the external magnetic field, here, the authors studied the directions of external
magnetic field in the plane of sample. Generally, the magnon-magnon coupling can also be realized by tilting
the field toward out-of-plane direction. The observed mode hoping can also appear when tilting the magnetic
field out-of-plane? It is appreciated if they can give a discussion.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. As the reviewer pointed out, out-of-plane (OOP)
magnetic fields can in some cases induce magnon–magnon coupling by lifting the degeneracy between optic
and acoustic modes [D. MacNeill et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 047204 (2019); A. H. Comstock et al., Nat.
Commun. 14, 1834 (2023)]. To clarify the role of OOP fields in our system, we conducted additional
measurements as follows.
First, we investigated whether magnon–magnon coupling could be induced in our SAF by applying a tilted
magnetic field. We measured FMR spectra with tilt angles of 90°, 60°, 30°, and 10° relative to the OOP
direction (see Fig. R1.3). Unlike previous reports on van der Waals magnets [e.g., Fig. 4 of MacNeill et al.,
PRL (2019); Fig. 3 of Comstock et al., Nat. Commun. (2023)], our measurements did not reveal any signature
of an anticrossing gap. Instead, we only observed a systematic shift of the mode crossing point toward higher
applied fields as the tilt angle increased, which we attribute to the change in the in-plane projection of the
external field. These results indicate that in our CoFeB/Ru/CoFeB SAF, an OOP field does not induce
symmetry breaking sufficient to generate magnon–magnon coupling.
Next, we examined whether an OOP field influences nonlinear mode hopping. We applied an OOP bias
field of 67 mT—comparable to the in-plane field used for mode-hopping measurements—and repeated the
experiments. As shown in Fig. R1.4, the spectra obtained with [Fig. R1.4b] and without [Fig. R1.4a] the OOP
field are nearly identical, confirming that the OOP field has negligible impact on mode hopping in our system.
We interpret these observations as follows. In our SAF, magnon–magnon coupling is mediated primarily
by dynamic dipolar interactions. The resulting anticrossing emerges when the magnetic field is applied in-
plane and is not collinear with the magnon propagation direction, providing the necessary symmetry breaking.
In contrast, prior studies of van der Waals antiferromagnets and low-symmetry layered magnets have shown
that OOP fields can break structural or parity symmetries, leading to gap opening. In those systems, intrinsic
asymmetries (e.g., inequivalent layers, inversion-symmetry breaking, or Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction)
allow OOP fields to couple the optic and acoustic modes.
Our CoFeB/Ru/CoFeB trilayer differs in key respects: the two ferromagnetic layers are nominally identical,
the Ru spacer only mediates interlayer exchange, and the system exhibits strong in-plane magnetic anisotropy.
As a result, the symmetry-breaking pathway for OOP-field–induced coupling is negligible. We therefore
conclude that in our SAF, the OOP magnetic field has negligible influence on both magnon–magnon coupling
and mode hopping.

mT. I suggest they chose the field at which the intensity of the optic and acoustic is similar.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. As the reviewer pointed out, showing a line
profile where the optic and acoustic modes have comparable intensity would indeed provide a clearer
illustration of the gap closing. We also considered this point and examined line profiles at various fields (see
Fig. R1.5). Among the fields tested, 27 mT provided the clearest signature of both peaks, which is why we
presented this line profile in the main text.
While it would be ideal to find a field where the optic and acoustic intensities are nearly equal, such a
condition does not occur in our system. Both modes are present across the entire field range, but the intensity
of the upper branch is always larger. This asymmetry arises from the different origins of the two signals: in
our SAF, the optic mode intensity corresponds to variations of the longitudinal component of magnetization
along the external field direction, whereas the acoustic mode corresponds to variations of the transverse
component. At low fields (nearly spin-flop state), the spins align almost perpendicular to the field, so the
longitudinal variation is large while the transverse variation is small—resulting in strong optic and weak
acoustic signals. At high fields (nearly spin-flip state), the spins align nearly parallel to the field, so the
transverse variation becomes dominant while the longitudinal variation is suppressed—leading to strong
acoustic and weaker optic signals. Consequently, the upper branch remains stronger throughout the entire field
range. We note that this behavior is consistent with previous reports, for example Y. Shiota et al., Phys. Rev.
Lett. 125, 017203 (2020).

optic to the acoustic mode, with a frequency drop as large as 4–5 GHz. We further show that this transition is
hysteretic, and we establish its microscopic origin through both theoretical modeling and micromagnetic
simulations. These features go beyond earlier demonstrations of nonlinear coupling by directly linking strong
nonlinearity to mode conversion and hysteresis.

magnonics but also carries potential for applications such as magnon-based mode converters and frequency
switches. Reviewer #1 also highlighted this point, noting that “the observed mode hopping and the hysteretic

they may help guide the development of a comprehensive theory and clarify the respective roles of Kittel and
